claim: Orf9b is an 11 kDa protein encoded through an alternative open reading frame within the N gene of both SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2.
source: Open Reading Frame 9b (Orf9b) is an 11 kDa protein encoded through an alternative open reading frame within the N gene of both SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction section of the manuscript.

claim: Orf9b localizes to the outer mitochondrial membrane during SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Orf9b localizes to the outer mitochondrial membrane during SARS-CoV and 2 infection (Meier et al., 2006; Gordon et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Large-scale interactome profiling of SARS-CoV-2 proteins identified Tom70 as interacting with Orf9b.
source: Large-scale interactome profiling of SARS-CoV-2 proteins identified the mitochondrial import receptor Tom70 (Translocase of Outer Membrane 70) as interacting with Orf9b (Gordon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gordon et al., 2020.

claim: Both SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2 Orf9b bind to Tom70 during infection and this is sufficient to suppress the IFN response in the absence of additional viral factors.
source: Both SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2 Orf9b have been shown to bind to Tom70 during infection, and this is sufficient to suppress the IFN response in the absence of additional viral factors (Jiang et al., 2020; Gordon et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cryo-EM and X-ray structures of SARS-CoV-2 Orf9b:Tom70 showed Orf9b as a monomeric amphipathic helix bound to Tom70 at the C-terminal MTS binding site in a 1:1 interaction.
source: Cryo-EM and X-ray structures of SARS-CoV-2 Orf9b:Tom70 showed Orf9b as a monomeric amphipathic helix bound to Tom70 at the C-terminal MTS binding site in a 1:1 interaction (Gordon et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Crystal structures of both SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2 show Orf9b adopting a β-sheet-rich homodimer.
source: This was surprising because the crystal structures of both SARS-CoV (Meier et al., 2006) and SARS-CoV-2 (Jin et al., 2023, 7YE7, 7YE8, and unpublished structure 6Z4U) show Orf9b adopting a β-sheet-rich homodimer.
evidence: This is supported by citations to crystal structures.

claim: The KD of Orf9b peptide:Tom70 binding is 653±2 nM as measured by SPR.
source: Global fitting of the Orf9b peptide:Tom70 binding curves resulted in a KD of 653±2 nM (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from SPR experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The association rate constant (kon) for Orf9b peptide:Tom70 is 6.2 × 10^4 M^-1s^-1 and the dissociation rate constant (koff) is 4.1 × 10^-2 s^-1.
source: These fits were associated with kinetic rates of kon = 6.2 × 104 M–1s–1 and koff = 4.1 × 10–2 s–1
evidence: These are kinetic parameters derived from SPR fitting.

claim: The KD of Orf9b-FITC:Tom70 binding is 288±1 nM as measured by SPR.
source: Globally fitting a 1:1 Langmuir binding model to Orf9b-FITC:Tom70 resulted in a KD of 288±1 nM with kinetic rates kon = 7.4 × 104 M–1s–1 and koff = 2.1 × 10–2 s–1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from SPR experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The KD of Orf9b-FITC:Tom70 binding is 240±7 nM as measured by fluorescence polarization.
source: Fitting with a 1:1 binding model yielded a KD of 240±7 nM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from fluorescence polarization experiments.

claim: The Ki of unlabeled Orf9b peptide is 880±5 nM as measured by competition fluorescence polarization.
source: We fit a one-site competitive binding model to this dataset, which yielded a Ki of 880±5 nM which is consistent with the SPR measurement of the KD for Orf9b peptide:Tom70 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from competition fluorescence polarization experiments.

claim: Orf9b S53E phosphomimetic mutation does not bind to Tom70.
source: As expected, we did not see any decrease in FP signal confirming that the S53E mutation directly blocks Orf9b from binding Tom70 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is experimental data from fluorescence polarization assays.

claim: The refolded Orf9b homodimer structure closely aligns with the lipid-bound reference structure with an RMSD of 1.1 Å.
source: Aligning the structure of the Orf9b homodimer (PDB 6Z4U) with our structure of the refolded Orf9b homodimer (9N55) in Pymol resulted in an RMSD of 1.1 Å.
evidence: This is a structural comparison result from crystallographic data.

claim: The refolded Orf9b homodimer does not have significant electron density in the central hydrophobic channel to support the placement of lipid.
source: As we hypothesized, when we inspected the central channel of the refolded homodimer, we did not observe significant electron density in the central hydrophobic channel to support the placement of the lipid but did observe some diffuse density peaks in both the Fo-Fc and 2Fo-Fc maps (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on crystallographic electron density analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: MS and MS/MS of extracted lipids confirmed that the bound lipids are 1-palmitoyl-sn-glycerol (MG 16:0) or 1-stearoyl-sn-glycerol (MG 18:0).
source: The MS and MS/MS of the extracted lipids confirmed that the bound lipids are 1-palmitoyl-sn-glycerol (MG 16:0) or 1-stearoyl-sn-glycerol (MG 18:0; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is experimental data from mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: The KD of apo-Orf9b homodimer dissociation is 1.2±0.1 µM as determined by size exclusion chromatography.
source: We fit the total concentration of Orf9b versus the fraction of Orf9b in the homodimer form with a non-linear regression and determined a KD of 1.2±0.1 uM (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is experimental data from size exclusion chromatography shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Lipid-bound Orf9b homodimer remains homodimeric at multiple concentrations.
source: In contrast, the lipid-bound homodimer remains homodimeric at multiple concentrations (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is experimental data from size exclusion chromatography shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The KD of Orf9b:Orf9b homodimerization is 4.4±0.7 µM as measured by SPR.
source: Global fitting of the binding curves using a 1:1 Langmuir binding model yielded a KD of 4.4±0.7 µM which is within the order of magnitude of the dissociation constant calculated by dilution (1.2±0.1 µM; Figure 3E).
evidence: This is experimental data from SPR measurements.

claim: The kinetic rates for Orf9b homodimerization are kon = 7.88 × 10^4 M^-1s^-1 and koff = 3.5 × 10^-1 s^-1.
source: The kinetic rates were kon = 7.88 × 104 M–1s–1 and koff = 3.5 × 10–1 s–1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: These are kinetic parameters derived from SPR fitting shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The KD for full-length apo-Orf9b:Tom70 is 190±1 nM as measured by SPR.
source: When we performed global fitting of our Orf9b-Tom70 sensograms, we found that a 1:1 interaction showed a good fit, yielding a KD for Orf9b:Tom70 of 190±1 nM.
evidence: This is experimental data from SPR measurements.

claim: Lipid binding to the Orf9b homodimer reduces the dimer dissociation rate approximately 100-fold.
source: We found that the binding of a lipid to the Orf9b homodimer biases the Orf9b monomer:dimer equilibrium towards the dimer by reducing the dimer dissociation rate ~100 fold.
evidence: This is a conclusion from kinetic modeling of experimental data.

claim: The lipid-bound homodimer dissociation rate is 1.0×10^-3 s^-1 as determined by kinetic modeling.
source: We found that the lipid-bound homodimer dataset could be modeled by lowering the homodimer dissociation rate to 1.0x10–3 s–1, which is nearly 2 orders of magnitude from the SPR derived value for refolded Orf9b of 3.5x10–1 s–1 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a parameter derived from kinetic modeling shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The modeled KD for lipid-bound Orf9b homodimer is approximately 13 nM.
source: Based on the fitted association and dissociation rates for the lipid-bound homodimer, our model suggests that the lipid-bound dissociation constant for the Orf9b homodimer drops to ~13 nM, which is ~100-fold stronger than the experimentally determined dissociation constant of 1.2–4.4 µM for the refolded homodimer (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a calculated value from kinetic modeling.

claim: Truncated Orf9b (Δ91-97) behaves as an obligate monomer in Tom70 binding assays.
source: We interpreted this to mean that the truncation to Orf9b results in a homodimer that is substantially less stable than the WT homodimer and that our experimental results are capturing a largely monomeric binding behavior to Tom70 without influence of the homodimer.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental fluorescence polarization data.

claim: Truncated Orf9b (Δ91-97) co-immunoprecipitates with Tom70 in HEK293T cells.
source: While both WT and truncated Orf9b co-immunoprecipitated with Tom70, Orf9b S50/53E showed no interaction, as expected (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation assays shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Truncated Orf9b (Δ91-97) suppresses IFN induction comparably to WT Orf9b.
source: For both WT and truncated Orf9b, we observed a decrease in the fold induction of IFN (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is experimental data from IFN reporter assays shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Orf9b S50/53E does not suppress IFN induction and shows comparable levels to empty vector control.
source: Again, as expected, the S50/53E construct showed comparable levels of IFN induction to the empty vector control.
evidence: This is experimental data from IFN reporter assays.

claim: The fusion construct (4xSGG) shows a decrease in IFN response comparable to WT and truncated Orf9b.
source: Surprisingly, the fusion construct showed a decrease in IFN response that was comparable to both WT and truncated Orf9b (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is experimental data from IFN reporter assays shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Lambda variant (P10S) has a modeled homodimer dissociation rate of 2.0×10^-2 s^-1 and a modeled KD of 0.25 µM.
source: Lambda (P10S) exhibited the most stable behavior as judged by the modeled homodimer dissociation rate of 2.0x10–2 s–1 (modeled KD = 0.25 uM) which is approximately tenfold tighter than both WT and Omicron datasets (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a parameter derived from kinetic modeling shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Delta variant (T60A) has a modeled dissociation constant of 12 µM.
source: We found that a dissociation constant of 12 µM (calculated by increasing homodimer koff to 0.9 s–1) with a solution that is at equilibrium between homodimer and monomers prior to chasing with the fluorescent complex yielded the closest fit (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a parameter derived from kinetic modeling shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The T60A mutation does not reduce the affinity between Orf9b and Tom70.
source: We repeated the SPR experiment as previously for WT (Figure 1B) and did not observe a decrease in the affinity between Orf9b T60A and Tom70. We interpret this to mean that the T60A mutation does not reduce the affinity between Orf9b and Tom70 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is experimental data from SPR measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: All Orf9b variants (Delta, Lambda, Omicron) retain their interaction with Tom70 in co-immunoprecipitation assays.
source: We performed Co-IP of the three variants as previously described and observed no noticeable differences in Tom70 binding across different VOCs, confirming that these mutations do not directly alter the affinity between Orf9b and Tom70 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation assays shown in Figure 6E.

claim: All Orf9b variants (Delta, Lambda, Omicron) have comparable IFN suppression to WT, showing approximately 50% reduction compared to empty vector control.
source: We performed the IFN assay as previously described and saw that compared to WT, all variants had a comparable decrease in the fold-induction of IFN, which was approximately 50% reduction compared to the empty vector control (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is experimental data from IFN reporter assays shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Orf9b can form homodimers in the absence of lipid.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that Orf9b homodimer lipid-binding is not limited to the cell types it is expressed in. We also conclude that the lipid can unbind when Orf9b is completely unfolded and that Orf9b can form homodimers in the absence of lipid.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from crystallographic and mass spectrometry data.

claim: Lipid binding stabilizes the Orf9b homodimer but is not necessary for its formation.
source: These results also suggest that the lipid binding is not necessary for Orf9b dimerization; however, we cannot definitively rule out the possibility that the presence of lipids can also induce Orf9b dimerization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from crystallographic data.

claim: Orf9b can be phosphorylated at S53 by a host kinase which prevents binding to Tom70.
source: First, Orf9b can be phosphorylated (Bouhaddou et al., 2020; Thorne et al., 2022) at S53 by a host kinase which prevents binding to Tom70, restoring IFN signaling.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Crystal structures of the Orf9b homodimer show a hydrophobic central channel occupied by a lipid-like ligand.
source: Second, crystal structures of the Orf9b homodimer show a hydrophobic central channel that runs the length of the dimer that is occupied by a lipid-like ligand (Meier et al., 2006; Jin et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to crystal structures.

claim: Lipids co-purified with recombinantly expressed Orf9b in both E. coli and mammalian cells.
source: This led to an initial characterization of the Orf9b homodimer as a membrane binding protein (Gao et al., 2021; Meier et al., 2006) with subsequent work showing that lipids co-purified with recombinantly expressed Orf9b in both E. coli and mammalian cells (Jin et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Separately purified Orf9b homodimer and Tom70 do not readily form an Orf9b:Tom70 complex.
source: Two groups have separately reported that the Orf9b:Tom70 complex formed by co-expressing the two proteins together (Gordon et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2021). Further, both reported that incubating separately purified Orf9b and Tom70 does not result in complex formation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Apo-Orf9b homodimer can be used to produce the Orf9b:Tom70 complex when incubated with Tom70.
source: We also confirmed that apo-Orf9b homodimer could be used to produce the Orf9b:Tom70 complex when incubated with Tom70.
evidence: This is experimental data from size exclusion chromatography shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The apo-Orf9b homodimer equilibrates rapidly (500-1000 s) with Orf9b-FITC:Tom70.
source: The apo-Orf9b homodimer equilibrated rapidly (500–1000 ss) with Orf9b-FITC:Tom70.
evidence: This is experimental data from fluorescence polarization kinetic assays.

claim: Lipid-bound Orf9b homodimer reaches equilibrium with Tom70 only after several hours of incubation.
source: Strikingly, we observed that the lipid-bound Orf9b homodimer was much slower to bind to Tom70 (as monitored by the decrease in fluorescent polarization) than for the apo protein, with equilibrium reached only after several hours of incubation (Figure 4Ai).
evidence: This is experimental data from fluorescence polarization kinetic assays shown in Figure 4Ai.

claim: Lipid binding does not affect the microscopic rate constant of Orf9b binding to Tom70.
source: Further, our model shows that lipid binding only acts on the rate of homodimer dissociation but does not affect the microscopic rate constant of Orf9b binding to Tom70 in our assay.
evidence: This is a conclusion from kinetic modeling of experimental data.

claim: Mutations in variants of concern can alter different microscopic rate constants without significantly affecting binding to Tom70.
source: We also found that mutations in variants of concern can alter different microscopic rate constants without significantly affecting binding to Tom70.
evidence: This is a conclusion from kinetic modeling and experimental data.

claim: Tom70 possesses two distinct binding sites: a C-terminal groove for amphipathic helices and an N-terminal chaperone binding site.
source: Tom70 possesses two distinct binding sites: a large C-terminal groove for the binding of amphipathic helices that form mitochondrial targeting sequences (MTS; Young et al., 2003; Backes et al., 2018) and an N-terminal chaperone binding site that recognizes the EEVD motif of Hsp70/90 (Young et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The loss of the chaperone binding site in Tom70 is sufficient to suppress IFN signaling.
source: In the context of IFN signaling, the loss of the chaperone binding site is sufficient to suppress IFN signaling (Lin et al., 2010; Wei et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: X-ray and Cryo-EM structures of the Orf9b:Tom70 complex show that R192 in Tom70 is displaced.
source: X-ray and Cryo-EM structures of the Orf9b:Tom70 complex show that a key residue in the N-terminal chaperone binding site of Tom70 (R192) is displaced, which was hypothesized to impair binding of chaperones during IFN signaling.
evidence: This is based on structural data from X-ray and Cryo-EM studies.

claim: When Orf9b is pre-bound to Tom70, peptides of the chaperone EEVD motif have reduced affinity.
source: In vitro studies have shown that when Orf9b is pre-bound to Tom70, peptides of the chaperone EEVD motif have a reduced affinity (Gao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Pre-binding of Hsp70 to the chaperone motif does not inhibit binding of MTS-containing substrates to the C-terminal domain of Tom70.
source: However, the pre-binding of Hsp70 to the chaperone motif does not inhibit binding of MTS-containing substrates to the C-terminal domain (Mills et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Orf9b has acquired mutations at both the protein and RNA level through several variants of concern.
source: In addition, Orf9b has acquired mutations at both the protein and RNA level through several variants of concern (VOC; Yang et al., 2023)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Mutations that regulate the expression of Orf9b result in increased expression at both transcriptomic and protein levels, leading to more potent suppression of IFN signaling.
source: Mutations that regulate the expression of Orf9b have been shown to result in an increase in the expression of Orf9b at both the transcriptomic and protein levels (Thorne et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023), which also leads to more potent suppression of IFN signaling.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MAVS functions as a scaffold for the recruitment of adaptor proteins that promote activation of transcription factors such as IRF3.
source: At the membrane, MAVS functions as a scaffold for the recruitment of additional adaptor proteins that promote the activation of transcription factors such as IRF3 that localize to the nucleus and drive the expression of innate immune genes such as IFN-β (Seth et al., 2005) inducing an antiviral state.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 viral infection triggers a weak type 1 interferon response.
source: A prominent feature of both SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2 is that viral infection triggers a weak type 1 interferon response (IFN-I; Blanco-Melo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The Orf9b peptide (residues 44-70) represents approximately ⅓ of the full-length Orf9b sequence.
source: This peptide represents approximately ⅓ of the full-length Orf9b sequence and can be used as a proxy for studying the behavior of the monomeric Orf9b intermediate.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The Orf9b peptide:Tom70 association rate is much slower than the diffusion limit.
source: The Orf9b peptide:Tom70 association rate was much slower than the diffusion limit, which may suggest that a conformational change occurs either by the peptide when adopting the helical conformation or by Tom70 to open up the C-terminal binding site.
evidence: This is an interpretation of SPR kinetic data.

claim: The FITC moiety on Orf9b-FITC slightly favors binding to Tom70 relative to the unlabeled peptide.
source: Fitting with a 1:1 binding model yielded a KD of 240±7 nM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), which is in good agreement with the SPR result and suggests that the FITC moiety slightly favors binding relative to the unlabeled peptide.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing SPR and fluorescence polarization data.

claim: S53 on Orf9b is positioned deep within the C-terminal Tom70 binding site.
source: S53 on Orf9b is positioned deep within the C-terminal Tom70 binding site and has been shown to undergo phosphorylation in cells infected with SARS-CoV-2 (Bouhaddou et al., 2020; Bouhaddou et al., 2023; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on structural data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The refolded Orf9b homodimer was crystallized in a different crystal form and space group than the reference structure.
source: Compared to the reference PDB structure, we were also able to resolve one of two disordered loops, which is likely due to the refolded homodimer crystallizing in a different crystal form and space group than the reference structure.
evidence: This is based on crystallographic data.

claim: The refolded Orf9b homodimer structure has a Z-score of 2.2 when compared to existing lipid-bound structures on the Dali server.
source: Further, we also searched our structures of the refolded Orf9b homodimer on the Dali server against the existing structures of the lipid-bound Orf9b homodimer, which yielded a Z-score of 2.2, which shows good correspondence between the structures.
evidence: This is a structural comparison result.

claim: Polder maps support the presence of an 8-carbon alkane in the natively folded Orf9b homodimer structure.
source: For the natively folded structure, the Polder maps clearly supported the presence of an 8-carbon alkane (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is based on crystallographic electron density analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Polder maps do not support the placement of an 8-carbon alkane in the refolded Orf9b homodimer structure.
source: however, for the refolded structure, Polder maps did not support the placement of the 8-carbon alkane (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on crystallographic electron density analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Glycine from crystallization buffer may occupy density peaks in the refolded Orf9b homodimer central channel.
source: We next modeled glycine into one of the density peaks and noted a good fit with little residual difference density (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C). Therefore, we conclude that the remaining density peaks in the channel are likely attributed to noise or crystallization buffer components.
evidence: This is based on crystallographic electron density analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The refolded Orf9b homodimer structure shows increased disorder compared to lipid-bound structures as judged by high B-factors and lower resolution.
source: The apo-Orf9b homodimer retains the same conformation as the lipid-bound structure, but we also observed an increased level of disorder as judged by the high B-factors and lower resolution of our structure when compared to published structures with lipids bound.
evidence: This is based on crystallographic data analysis.

claim: Residues 91-97 of the C-terminal tail on chain A form backbone hydrogen bonds with residues 50-56 of chain B in the Orf9b homodimer.
source: We investigated the homodimer interface and observed that residues 91–97 of the C-terminal tail on chain A form backbone hydrogen bonds with residues 50–56 of chain B (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Truncating the 7 C-terminal amino acids of Orf9b compromises the ability to form stable homodimers.
source: Our choice to truncate the 7 C-terminal amino acids was driven by the structure of the Orf9b homodimer which indicated that the 7 C-terminal residues form ⅔ of the homodimer interface; therefore, truncating them would compromise the ability for Orf9b to form stable homodimers and impede lipid binding.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural analysis.

claim: The N-terminus of each Orf9b chain is approximately 28 Å from the C-terminus of the opposite chain in the homodimer.
source: By examining structures of Orf9b homodimer, we observed that the N-terminus of each chain is approximately 28 Å from the C-terminus of the opposite chain (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The Orf9b fusion construct could not be successfully refolded to eliminate co-purifying lipids.
source: We attempted to refold the fusion homodimer to eliminate the co-purification of lipids; however, we were unable to recover the fusion homodimer.
evidence: This is a description of an experimental result.

claim: The fusion construct shows reduced Orf9b monomer:Tom70 association rate (approximately 10-fold) compared to WT.
source: We observe that the Orf9b monomer:Tom70 association rate is altered approximately 10-fold to 7.0x103 M–1s–1 while the dissociation rate remains unchanged compared to WT (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a parameter derived from kinetic modeling shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The fusion construct shows a 160-fold reduction in homodimer association rate compared to WT.
source: Additionally, the fused homodimer association rate (which can be viewed as a rate of tertiary complex formation) is reduced 160-fold compared to WT.
evidence: This is a parameter derived from kinetic modeling.

claim: The fusion construct shows approximately 1000-fold slower homodimer dissociation rate than WT lipid-bound rate.
source: Interestingly, the homodimer dissociation rate (or the tertiary unfolding rate) is also approximately 1000-fold slower than even the WT lipid-bound rate.
evidence: This is a parameter derived from kinetic modeling.

claim: The Orf9b fusion construct interacts with Tom70 in co-immunoprecipitation assays.
source: Surprisingly, we observed that the Orf9b fusion also interacted with Tom70.
evidence: This is experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation assays.

claim: Delta variant has a T60A mutation within the region of Orf9b that folds into the helix to bind Tom70.
source: While the Delta variant possesses a T60A mutation, which is within the region of Orf9b that folds into the helix to bind Tom70, the Lambda and Omicron variants have mutations outside the Tom70 binding region.
evidence: This is a description of mutations in variants of concern.

claim: Lambda and Omicron variants share a P10S mutation.
source: They share a P10S mutation, with Omicron also having a truncation of ∆27–29 within a disordered loop of the homodimer (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a description of mutations in variants of concern shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Omicron variant has a truncation of residues 27-29 in addition to the P10S mutation.
source: They share a P10S mutation, with Omicron also having a truncation of ∆27–29 within a disordered loop of the homodimer (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a description of mutations in variants of concern shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Omicron variant (P10S, ∆27-29) has a modeled homodimer dissociation rate of 2.5×10^-1 s^-1 and a modeled KD of 3.1 µM.
source: From our model, we observed that Omicron (P10S, ∆27–29) could be modeled with a homodimer dissociation rate of 2.5x10–1 s–1 which yielded a modeled KD of 3.1 µM which is close to the experimentally determined KD of the refolded WT dimer suggesting that the P10S, ∆27–29 mutations may have a minor effect on homodimer stability (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a parameter derived from kinetic modeling shown in Figure 6B.

claim: T60 in Orf9b makes a hydrogen bond with the backbone carbonyl between A68 and F69 of the same chain.
source: For Delta, the T60A mutation is present within the β-strand that is responsible for refolding into the ɑ-helix and binding to Tom70 (Figure 6D). T60 makes a hydrogen bond with the backbone carbonyl between A68 and F69 of the same chain which may contribute to the local stability of the β-strand.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The P10S mutation introduces a serine that forms several hydrogen bonds with R13 and the backbone carbonyl of A11 and L48.
source: For Lambda and Omicron, the P10S mutation results in the serine being positioned to form several hydrogen bonds between R13 and the backbone carbonyl of A11 and L48 within the same chain, which may contribute to local stability.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: The P10S mutation stabilizes the Orf9b homodimer, but the ∆27-29 truncation in Omicron counteracts this effect.
source: The Omicron variant additionally has a truncation of residues 27–29 within a disordered loop. Although the modeled homodimer dissociation rate was close to WT, the modeled KD was slightly lower, which was consistent between biological replicates, suggesting that the P10S mutation is stabilizing the homodimer like the Lambda variant, but the truncation of residues 27–29 may counteract this effect by destabilizing the homodimer.
evidence: This is an interpretation of kinetic modeling results.

claim: Mutations in VOC do not alter the association rate of the Orf9b:Tom70 complex.
source: Our in vitro kinetic model results showed that while mutations to Orf9b present in VOC can alter the stability of the Orf9b homodimer as modeled by the homodimer dissociation rate, they did not alter the association rate of the Orf9b:Tom70 complex (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a conclusion from kinetic modeling shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Mutations in VOC do not affect Orf9b-mediated suppression of type 1 interferon response relative to WT.
source: These results lead us to conclude that the mutations present in variants of concern may alter the Orf9b homodimerization kinetics, but they do not noticeably affect the interaction between Orf9b and Tom70 or Orf9b-mediated suppression of type 1 interferon response.
evidence: This is a conclusion from co-IP and IFN assay data.

claim: AlphaFold predictions of monomeric Orf9b show two helices: one encompassing residues 11-28 and another encompassing residues 44-70.
source: This idea was motivated by AlphaFold predictions of monomeric WT Orf9, which show two helices: the first encompassing residues 11–28 and the second encompassing residues 44–70 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on AlphaFold structural predictions shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The 11-28aa peptide of Orf9b does not bind to Tom70.
source: To test this idea, we generated a peptide for 11-28aa, but did not observe any signal for binding by the FP assay or SPR (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is experimental data from FP and SPR assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: The difference between Orf9b peptide and full-length kinetics is due to the peptide truncating residues responsible for binding to Tom70.
source: With only single-site binding, we speculate that the difference between the Orf9b peptide and full-length kinetics is due to the Orf9b peptide truncating several residues that are responsible for binding to Tom70 that influence both the association and dissociation pathways.
evidence: This is a speculation based on kinetic data.

claim: The model parameter ka (β-sheet to α-helix conversion rate) is a second-order rate constant.
source: We found that when the β-sheet to α-helix rate (ka) was made a second-order rate constant, we were able to hold the rate constant across all concentrations tested, suggesting a non-linearity in the monomer β-sheet concentration.
evidence: This is a conclusion from kinetic modeling.

claim: The model parameter kB (α-helix to β-sheet conversion rate) is a first-order rate constant.
source: We found that this model adequately described the changes in kinetic behavior for different concentrations of Orf9b, assuming the conversion of helix to β-sheet depended linearly on the concentration of Orf9b α-monomer with a first-order rate constant kB.
evidence: This is a conclusion from kinetic modeling.

claim: Under low concentrations of Orf9b homodimer, binding to Tom70 is limited by the rate of homodimer association and dissociation and the conversion of Orf9b monomers to the α-helical conformation.
source: Therefore, under low concentrations of Orf9b homodimer, binding to Tom70 is limited by the rate of homodimer association and dissociation as well as the conversion of Orf9b monomers to the α-helical conformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from sensitivity analysis of the kinetic model.

claim: Under high homodimer concentrations, the limiting step becomes the rate at which Orf9b-FITC dissociates from Tom70.
source: Under high homodimer conditions, the limiting step becomes the rate at which Orf9b-FITC dissociates from Tom70.
evidence: This is a conclusion from sensitivity analysis of the kinetic model.

claim: Orf9b is capable of binding to MAVS by co-immunoprecipitation.
source: Indeed, Orf9b has already been shown to be capable of binding to MAVS by Co-IP (Han et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: MAVS undergoes post-translational palmitoylation which affects its ability to localize to the mitochondrial outer membrane during viral infection.
source: As a post-translational modification (referred to as S-acylation), MAVS, a mitochondrial type 1 IFN signaling protein that associates with Tom70 (Liu et al., 2010; McWhirter et al., 2005; Seth et al., 2005), has been shown to be post-translationally palmitoylated, which affects its ability to localize to the mitochondrial outer membrane during viral infection and is a known target of Orf9b (Bu et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2025).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: When MAVS palmitoylation is impaired, IFN activation is impaired.
source: When this is impaired (either by mutation or by depletion of the palmitoylation enzyme ZDHHC24), IFN activation is impaired (Bu et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Orf9b is encoded through an alternative open reading frame within the nucleocapsid (N) gene.
source: Assigning a functional role to these mutations is complicated by the fact that Orf9b is encoded through an alternative open reading frame within the nucleocapsid (N) gene (Rota et al., 2003; Marra et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Coding mutations to the N gene are picked up by the coding region of Orf9b.
source: Orf9b is encoded through an alternative open reading frame within the N gene of SARS CoV 1 and 2, which results in coding mutations to N being picked up by the coding region of Orf9b.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the overlapping reading frames.

claim: The Omicron variant has mutations N: P13L and Orf9b: P10S.
source: These mutations include Omicron (N: P13L; Orf9b: P10S), Delta (N: D63G; Of9b: T60A), and Lambda (N:∆30–32, P13L; Orf9b:∆27–29, P10S) (Thorne et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The Delta variant has mutations N: D63G and Orf9b: T60A.
source: These mutations include Omicron (N: P13L; Orf9b: P10S), Delta (N: D63G; Of9b: T60A), and Lambda (N:∆30–32, P13L; Orf9b:∆27–29, P10S) (Thorne et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The Lambda variant has mutations N:∆30-32, P13L and Orf9b:∆27-29, P10S.
source: These mutations include Omicron (N: P13L; Orf9b: P10S), Delta (N: D63G; Of9b: T60A), and Lambda (N:∆30–32, P13L; Orf9b:∆27–29, P10S) (Thorne et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Lipid binding to Orf9b may occur at a later stage of infection or be sub-saturating the Orf9b homodimer population.
source: Therefore, if lipid binding occurs either at a later stage of infection or is sub-saturating the Orf9b homodimer population, it may not noticeably affect IFN signaling as the copies of Orf9b bound to Tom70 remain tightly associated.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the kinetic model and experimental data.

claim: Copies of Orf9b bound to Tom70 remain tightly associated and may become kinetically trapped.
source: Further, the tight affinity between Orf9b and Tom70 may suggest that upon binding, Orf9b becomes kinetically trapped to Tom70 and does not fully revert to the homodimer conformation, resulting in the immediate suppression of IFN.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the kinetic data.

claim: Residual interaction between Orf9b fusion and Tom70 may be sufficient to drive IFN suppression without saturating Tom70.
source: Unlike the S50/53E mutant, which directly alters the microscopic rate constant between Orf9b and Tom70, our model of the fusion construct suggests that the microscopic affinity of Orf9b for Tom70 is also manipulated by rate constants that describe the interconversion between both secondary structures and tertiary structures but does not fully inhibit binding. Therefore, it is possible that even a residual interaction between Orf9b and Tom70 may be sufficient to drive a suppression of IFN without necessarily saturating Tom70.
evidence: This is a speculation based on kinetic modeling and cellular assay results.

claim: Not all copies of Orf9b homodimer may be bound to lipids in cells.
source: One possibility that emerges is that while lipid binding to the Orf9b homodimer does occur in cells (as supported by our mass spectrometry results), not all copies of the homodimer are bound to lipids.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the discrepancy between in vitro and cellular results.

claim: Free copies of monomeric Orf9b or apo-Orf9b homodimer may be available to bind Tom70 in cells.
source: This would leave free copies of either monomeric Orf9b or apo-Orf9b homodimer available to bind to Tom70 and result in suppressed IFN signaling.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain cellular assay results.

claim: The homodimer conformation of Orf9b may be capable of antagonizing other IFN signaling factors such as MAVS by binding to palmitoyl groups.
source: Therefore, future investigations should consider if the homodimer conformation of Orf9b is capable of antagonizing other IFN signaling factors such as MAVS by binding to palmitoyl groups.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research based on the lipid-binding properties of Orf9b.
